findings.where: the thread, between the 'hold · Thu 3 Sep · 20:46' note and the 'a squeeze · Thu 3 Sep · 20:51' note; extracted frames 169 through 254 of 518
findings.what: The one plain text message that crosses in this clip never becomes readable: from frame 169 to frame 254 (86 frames, 1.38 s of app time at the clip's 16 ms step, measured by stepping the extracted frames) it sits on the desk as a flat blank sheet carrying only the word 'teo' — the reader's own name — with no text, no timestamp and no delivery mark, and its words appear nowhere in the clip's 518 frames; logs/08_state_propagating.json far[2] records 'message it is raining here too' sent at frame 165, and the scene's own report ends with fold.playhead 0 of 139 with 24 frames decoded.
findings.why: The rubric asks whether every messenger capability is dependable and whether any state stalls; in the one clip whose subject is a thing crossing between the two devices, the message arrives and stays shut, so a reader stepping the clip cannot tell what was said or even that anything was said — while every feeling in the same clip (hold 20:46, a squeeze 20:51, here 20:54) lands already legible with a timestamp.

findings.where: 13: the first note under the pinned standing line, y = 285 to 410 of 3120. 02_chat: the top of the thread, a torn edge at y = 285 to 300 of 3120 with no paper body below the standing line
findings.what: The record over-counts what a reader can see, and it over-counts the state the row cares most about. logs/13_messenger_states.report.json states_on_the_glass = {read 1, sent 2, 'it would not go' 1}, but the row it names as read (0001M4GW48FEW3M67XKAZT5051) is on the glass only as a 125-device-pixel blank sliver of paper with its ink and its whole margin row above the frame's top edge — I scanned all 3120 rows of the 1440x3120 frame and there is no 'read' word or double tick anywhere in it. The same clipping costs 02_chat.png one of its four: the report counts read 4, the frame carries three legible 'read' marks (16:40 on the 0:26 voice note, 17:14, 19:34) and the fourth row is present only as a ragged dark edge.
findings.why: 'Delivery and read state' is named in the row, and 13_messenger_states.png is the single artifact whose job is to show the messenger's states; it shows sent twice and 'it would not go' once and no read at all, so the read marker cannot be checked against the picture in the place the capture says to check it — the same class of record-versus-picture drift the code at app/lib/regions/chat/note.dart:305 says was already found once.

findings.what: The only per-frame cost measurement in the whole capture is over budget on every frame: build+raster exceeds 16 ms on 793 of 793 frames (100 per cent), median 123 ms, p90 803 ms, p99 1613 ms, max 1815 ms. Raster is defensibly inflated (p50 106 ms, software rasteriser, and the log says so). Build is not covered by that excuse: p50 4 ms but p90 671 ms, p99 1489 ms, max 1676 ms, and the shape is a 700-1500 ms build on roughly one frame in four, steady the whole way through rather than a warm-up (frames 0-49 mean 431 ms, 750-792 mean 152 ms; every 50-frame block has 10 or more frames over 100 ms). Nothing bounds this on real hardware: frames.json scroll_emulator is {'missing': 'no Android device was up in this session'}, so there is no on-device or GPU frame cost anywhere in the evidence, and the clip itself cannot show the fault by construction — BRIEFING.md says each frame is one step of a driven clock, so a frame that took 1.8 s to draw still occupies 16 ms of the clip.
findings.why: 'No scroll jank against the year-deep seeded history' is named in the row; the clip's smoothness is a property of the driven clock rather than of the frame budget, and the one budget measurement in evidence says the app's own build phase, which no GPU would have helped, blows the frame on a quarter of the frames.

findings.where: the top-level transport field, every scene report's sync.link.address, and the tailscale.later_check block
findings.what: Every capability check in this capture ran on loopback, not on the wire the couple would use. reliability.json says transport 'local' and each scene report says transport 'local' with address http://127.0.0.1:8480. The tailnet crossing inside the same file is dated checked_at 2026-09-05T00:28:43Z and its later_check is {'status': 'pending', 'why': 'the nodes were not answering when this was re-run'} stamped 2026-09-09T04:59:48Z — this capture's own morning; coldstart.json is the same, written 2026-09-05 with a pending re-check on 2026-09-09.
findings.why: The nineteen capability claims that carry this row's hardest properties — offline_queue '26 events queued offline, all delivered on reconnect', reconnect_ordering 'seq 1..173 gapless and monotonic after the gap', kill_mid_send, draft_survival, host_offline_outbox — are all measured over a socket in the same process tree, and the only measurement over the real transport failed to reproduce on the day of the capture, so 'correct ordering after going offline and reconnecting' rests on a four-day-old record.

findings.where: states_on_the_glass across all reports: 02_chat {read 4}, 06_unfolding {sent 1}, 13_messenger_states {read 1, sent 2, 'it would not go' 1}, 10_first_run {}
findings.what: Two of the five delivery states the app defines are drawn in no artifact. app/lib/spine/projections/thread.dart declares queued ('waiting to send'), sending ('going'), sent, read and refused ('it would not go'); only sent, read and 'it would not go' appear anywhere in the capture. The mark for a message waiting in the outbox and the mark for a message on its way exist in the source and in no picture.
findings.why: Those are precisely the two states a person sees when the link is down, which is the moment the row is about; with no artifact showing them, the offline behaviour claimed in reliability.json cannot be checked against a picture at all.

findings.where: the four result rows below the filter chips, with PHOTOGRAPHS underlined as the active type
findings.what: A search restricted to photographs returns no photographs. logs/12_search.report.json gives query 'morning', hits 6, kinds {photo: 6}; every visible result is a prose line ('you sent a photograph — eight in the morning. six weeks ago this was black and I was walking to a car park by feel') with the matched word highlighted, and there is not one thumbnail in the frame.
findings.why: The row names media search; finding a picture from last spring means reading four captions and opening them one at a time, which is the errand people open Instagram to avoid.

findings.where: the bottom of the masonry, the middle and right columns at roughly y = 2700 to 2930 of 3120, above the tab strip and fully on the glass
findings.what: Two tiles of the gallery are bare paper with nothing on them. The report says tiles_built 26 with blobs asked 18, arrived 18, waiting 0, so eight built tiles have not asked for a picture yet and two of them are inside the frame.

findings.artifact: MANIFEST.json missing block, and every scene log's load field
findings.where: 09_two_devices.png and 16_setup_android.png; logs/01_pulse.json load {ms 8240, store fresh} against the warm loads of 2016-2316 ms
findings.what: No picture in the set shows two devices, and no picture shows what is on the screen while the app loads. The reason given for the two absent artifacts is measured rather than asserted — no /dev/kvm, adbd answered after 113 minutes and the framework never came up behind it — and I accept it as a reason; the consequence is still that delivery and read state, which are two-device properties, are shown only from one side. Separately the fresh-store cold start is 8.24 s and every warm launch is 2.0 to 2.3 s, and no artifact covers those seconds.
findings.why: 'No spinner that outstays its welcome' cannot be judged either way from this evidence, and the two-device behaviour the row turns on is visible only in JSON.

what_is_working: The dense scroll is exactly as smooth as it is claimed to be, and I measured it rather than taking the log's word. Template-matching a 140x780 patch with zero-mean normalised correlation across all 299 consecutive frame pairs of 11_chat_scroll.mp4 gives an on-screen displacement that matches logs/11_chat_scroll.fling.json's moved x 3 (dpr 3) to within 0.93 device pixels on the worst pair, mean 0.34; no pair is off by more than 2 px; mean correlation 0.980; smallest step 31 device px, largest 143. The fling log's own accounting is exact too: asked equals moved on all 300 frames to the last decimal, no frame under a device pixel, no backward step.

Stitching those 299 measured offsets into a single 26,584-pixel panorama of the thread produces a seamless, coherent year: no tearing at any join, timestamps strictly increasing across 10.8 screens (Wed 22 Apr 21:40 through Mon 27 Apr 20:40), no repeated message, no gap in the conversation, no blank row, and not one instance of the 'still fetching the picture.' placeholder that app/lib/regions/chat/blob_widgets.dart can draw.

Every capability the row names is visible somewhere in the set: text throughout; a photograph in the thread ('The car park at eight', taped at one corner, in 11_chat_scroll); video with real transport in 14_media_viewer (pause, a scrub thumb, 0:01 / 0:03, caption on its own slip, 'put it back'); a voice note with waveform, play triangle and 0:26 in 02_chat and six more in 04_moments; a reaction folded onto its target rather than given a row of its own; a reply in the composer with the quoted line and a cancel; typing indication ('noor writing...') in 13, 06, 08 and 11; 'edited' with a turn-back caret; a delete that leaves 'took this back' as a stub; and search with type, author and range filters.

The delivery marks that are drawn are legible and genuinely distinct: 'sent' with one tick, 'read' with two, and 'it would not go' with a red cross and the reason kept on the paper rather than in a toast.

Ordering and non-duplication hold everywhere I could check them against pixels: the panorama is monotonic over 10.8 screens; in 06_unfolding.mp4 a message arriving from the far phone lands at 'Thu 3 Sep · 19:45', correctly after the 19:40 rows already on the desk, and becomes fully legible 155 frames (2.48 s of app time) after the far side sent it; reliability.json records 175 events on both sides, 0 duplicates, same order both sides, monotonic.

You can tell who wrote what without a name on every note: two clearly different hands, different paper stocks, and read marks only on your own side. logs/hand.json backs the hand up numerically — 513 marks of ink on 02_chat.png, twin share 0.058 at IoU 0.85 and 0.0 at 0.99, so nothing is a font repeating itself.

Notification behaviour is granular and honestly evidenced: 05_settings.png shows per-event-type routing (wake me / quietly / not at all) with a quiet window 23:00-07:00, and crops/reception*.png shows one delivered end to end with logs/reception.json stating plainly that it is Chromium on a Linux virtual display and not an iPhone banner.
verdict: The messenger is real and most of it is dependable: I measured the year-deep scroll myself rather than trusting the log, and it holds up — 299 of 299 frame pairs move on screen by what the framework says it asked for, to within a device pixel, and the 26,584-pixel panorama I stitched from those offsets is a seamless, strictly ordered, gap-free year with no duplicate row and no fetch placeholder in it. Text, photos, video, voice notes, reactions, replies, typing, edit, delete, search and the media viewer are all visible in the set and drawn with care. What keeps this below its floor is that the properties which actually decide whether the couple leaves Instagram are the ones the pictures do not carry. In 08_state_propagating.mp4, the one clip about a thing crossing between the two phones, the one text message that crosses stays shut for 86 frames as a blank sheet with the reader's own name on it and never opens anywhere in the clip's 518 frames. In 13_messenger_states.png, the artifact whose only job is the messenger's states, the read marker is recorded and not drawn — the row it names is a 125-pixel blank sliver clipped at the top edge, and the same clipping costs 02_chat.png one of its four, so the record over-counts the picture on exactly the state the row names. Two of the five delivery states — the message waiting in the outbox and the message on its way — exist in the source and in no frame. And every capability check in this capture ran on loopback; the only crossing over the real transport is dated four days before the capture and its re-check that morning came back pending because the nodes were not answering. So: no dropped or duplicated message anywhere I could see, no jank in the pixels, ordering correct — but the offline, reconnect and two-device behaviour that the category turns on is a JSON claim in this run, not a picture, and the one picture of a message arriving shows it arriving unreadable.
